- When sentiment is high (≥0.8) and forecast is trending up, reduce forecast peak by 5–10% to avoid over-optimism.  
- When sentiment is low (≤0.4) and forecast is trending down, avoid excessive downward correction — allow slight mean reversion but don’t overshoot below 1–2σ below recent mean.  
- If recent price history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days falling), model should not forecast further decline — instead, adjust downward slope to match recent trend.  
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), forecast should not immediately follow with a spike — instead, apply a lagged correction (e.g., 2–3 days of smoothing) to avoid overshoot.  
- If sentiment is mixed (0.4–0.8) and forecast is diverging from recent 10-day average, align forecast to 10-day moving average with ±1–2% buffer.  
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is consistently bullish, reduce forecast by 2–3% to account for market overreaction.  
- If sentiment is bearish and price is trending up, reduce forecast slope — don’t let model chase sentiment-driven rallies.  
- Always check if forecast is within 1–2σ of recent 10-day mean — if not, adjust to avoid extreme outliers.
